Cancel every

*outstanding*durable wait for`session_id` without
deleting the session: each waiter receives a terminal
[instead of hanging, late resolves observe that terminal, and waits registered afterwards behave normally — in contrast to](https://docs.rs/lash-core/0.1.0-alpha.82/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lash_core/runtime/effect/executor/enum.Resolution.html#variant.Cancelled)`Resolution::Cancelled`[, which tombstones the session’s waits forever.](https://docs.rs/lash-core/0.1.0-alpha.82/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lash_core/runtime/effect/executor/trait.AwaitEventResolver.html#method.revoke_await_events_for_session)`revoke_await_events_for_session`[Read more](https://docs.rs/lash-core/0.1.0-alpha.82/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lash_core/runtime/effect/executor/trait.AwaitEventResolver.html#method.cancel_await_events_for_session)[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lash_postgres_store/postgres/effect_replay.rs.html#595-623)

Checkpoint-rooted mark/sweep over `lash_blobs`, mirroring the SQLite
store’s semantics ([ GcReport](https://docs.rs/lash-core/0.1.0-alpha.82/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lash_core/store/struct.GcReport.html) fields match). Postgres inlines the
tool/plugin/execution snapshots inside each checkpoint envelope, so

`lash_blobs` holds only checkpoint envelopes and the reachable set is the
set of live checkpoint refs (plus any child artifact ref an envelope
still names — usually none, but retained defensively). The three
Lashlang artifact namespaces live in a separate, upsert-in-place table
(`lash_lashlang_artifacts`) that never orphans, so GC does not touch it.[§](https://docs.rs#method.tombstone_nodes)#### fn [tombstone_nodes](https://docs.rs/lash-core/0.1.0-alpha.82/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lash_core/store/trait.StoreMaintenance.html#tymethod.tombstone_nodes)<'life0, 'life1, 'async_trait>(

}## Expand description

Connection-pool and per-connection timeout knobs for [ PostgresStorage](https://docs.rs/struct.PostgresStorage.html).

Mutating session work first claims the durable session execution lease.
Session commits then verify that lease fence and use **optimistic CAS** on
the head (`UPDATE … WHERE head_revision = expected`) as a stale-writer
backstop, not as the normal cross-worker concurrency primitive.
`lock_timeout` is defense in depth: it caps how long the fenced CAS write
may wait on the head row’s lock before erroring (surfaced as a retryable
conflict), so a pathological burst can never starve the pool.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.max_connections)

`max_connections: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)Maximum pooled connections. Default 16.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.min_connections)

`min_connections: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)Minimum idle connections kept warm. Default 0.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.acquire_timeout)

`acquire_timeout: `[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)How long `acquire` waits for a free connection before erroring. Default 30s.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.idle_timeout)

`idle_timeout: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)>Close a connection after this idle period. Default 10m.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.max_lifetime)

`max_lifetime: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)>Recycle a connection after this lifetime. Default 30m.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.lock_timeout)

`lock_timeout: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)>Postgres `lock_timeout` applied to every connection. Default 10s.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.statement_timeout)

`statement_timeout: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)>Postgres `statement_timeout` applied to every connection. Default 30s — a
backstop so a wedged query can never hold a connection indefinitely.

# base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/^0.22/

## Expand description

Correct, fast, and configurable [base64](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Base64) decoding and encoding. Base64
transports binary data efficiently in contexts where only plain text is
allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Use an [ Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html) to decode or encode base64, configured with the base64
alphabet and padding behavior best suited to your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#engine-setup)Engine setup

There is more than one way to encode a stream of bytes as “base64”.
Different applications use different encoding
[alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding behaviors](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-alphabet)Encoding alphabet

Almost all base64 [alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) use `A-Z`, `a-z`, and
`0-9`, which gives nearly 64 characters (26 + 26 + 10 = 62), but they differ
in their choice of their final 2.

Most applications use the [standard](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.STANDARD.html) alphabet specified
in [RFC 4648](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-4).  If that’s all you need, you can get started
quickly by using the pre-configured
[ STANDARD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.STANDARD.html) engine, which is also available
in the

[module as shown here, if you prefer a minimal](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use`
footprint.```
use base64::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.decode(b"+uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "/+wgVQA=");
```
Other common alphabets are available in the [ alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#url-safe-alphabet)URL-safe alphabet

The standard alphabet uses `+` and `/` as its two non-alphanumeric tokens,
which cannot be safely used in URL’s without encoding them as `%2B` and
`%2F`.

To avoid that, some applications use a [“URL-safe” alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.URL_SAFE.html),
which uses `-` and `_` instead. To use that alternative alphabet, use the
[ URL_SAFE](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.URL_SAFE.html) engine. This example doesn’t
use

[to show what a more explicit](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use` would look like.```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.decode(b"-uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "_-wgVQA=");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#padding-characters)Padding characters

Each base64 character represents 6 bits (2⁶ = 64) of the original binary data, and every 3 bytes of input binary data will encode to 4 base64 characters (8 bits × 3 = 6 bits × 4 = 24 bits).

When the input is not an even multiple of 3 bytes in length, [canonical](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-3.5)
base64 encoders insert padding characters at the end, so that the output
length is always a multiple of 4:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg==");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8=");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
Canonical encoding ensures that base64 encodings will be exactly the same,
byte-for-byte, regardless of input length. But the `=` padding characters
aren’t necessary for decoding, and they may be omitted by using a
[ NO_PAD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.NO_PAD.html) configuration:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
The pre-configured `NO_PAD` engines will reject inputs containing padding
`=` characters. To encode without padding and still accept padding while
decoding, create an [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with
that [padding mode](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.DecodePaddingMode.html).

`assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.decode(b"Zm8="), Err(base64::DecodeError::InvalidPadding));`[§](https://docs.rs#further-customization)Further customization

Decoding and encoding behavior can be customized by creating an
[engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with an [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding configuration](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html):

```
use base64::{engine, alphabet, Engine as _};
// bizarro-world base64: +/ as the first symbols instead of the last
let alphabet =
    alphabet::Alphabet::new("+/ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789")
    .unwrap();
// a very weird config that encodes with padding but requires no padding when decoding...?
let crazy_config = engine::GeneralPurposeConfig::new()
    .with_decode_allow_trailing_bits(true)
    .with_encode_padding(true)
    .with_decode_padding_mode(engine::DecodePaddingMode::RequireNone);
let crazy_engine = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet, crazy_config);
let encoded = crazy_engine.encode(b"abc 123");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-allocation)Memory allocation

The [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and [encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) engine methods
allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
`encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding)Decoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::decode` | returns a new `Vec<u8>` | always |
| `Engine::decode_vec` | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::decode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding)Encoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::encode` | returns a new `String` | always |
| `Engine::encode_string` | appends to provided `String` | if `String`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::encode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#input-and-output)Input and output

The `base64` crate can [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and
[encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) values in memory, or
[ DecoderReader](https://docs.rs/read/struct.DecoderReader.html) and

[provide streaming decoding and encoding for any](https://docs.rs/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html)

`EncoderWriter`[readable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)or

[writable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)byte stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding-1)Decoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
let mut input = io::stdin();
let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-1)Encoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
let mut output = io::stdout();
let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#display)Display

If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) trait, use

[:](https://docs.rs/display/struct.Base64Display.html)

`Base64Display````
use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.

# reqwest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reqwest/^0.13/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#reqwest)reqwest

The `reqwest` crate provides a convenient, higher-level HTTP
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html).

It handles many of the things that most people just expect an HTTP client to do for them.

- Async and [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)Clients
- Plain bodies, [JSON](https://docs.rs#json),[urlencoded](https://docs.rs#forms),[multipart](https://docs.rs/multipart/index.html)
- Customizable [redirect policy](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)
- HTTP [Proxies](https://docs.rs#proxies)
- Uses [TLS](https://docs.rs#tls)by default
- Cookies

The [ reqwest::Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) is asynchronous (requiring Tokio). For
applications wishing  to only make a few HTTP requests, the

[API may be more convenient.](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)

`reqwest::blocking`Additional learning resources include:

[§](https://docs.rs#commercial-support)Commercial Support

For private advice, support, reviews, access to the maintainer, and the
like, reach out for [commercial support](https://seanmonstar.com/sponsor).

[§](https://docs.rs#making-a-get-request)Making a GET request

For a single request, you can use the [ get](https://docs.rs/fn.get.html) shortcut method.

```
let body = reqwest::get("https://www.rust-lang.org")
    .await?
    .text()
    .await?;
println!("body = {body:?}");
```
**NOTE**: If you plan to perform multiple requests, it is best to create a
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) and reuse it, taking advantage of keep-alive connection
pooling.

[§](https://docs.rs#making-post-requests-or-setting-request-bodies)Making POST requests (or setting request bodies)

There are several ways you can set the body of a request. The basic one is
by using the `body()` method of a [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html). This lets you set the
exact raw bytes of what the body should be. It accepts various types,
including

`String` and `Vec<u8>`. If you wish to pass a custom
type, you can use the `reqwest::Body` constructors.```
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .body("the exact body that is sent")
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#forms)Forms

It’s very common to want to send form data in a request body. This can be done with any type that can be serialized into form data.

This can be an array of tuples, or a `HashMap`, or a custom type that
implements [ Serialize](http://serde.rs).

The feature `form` is required.

```
// This will POST a body of `foo=bar&baz=quux`
let params = [("foo", "bar"), ("baz", "quux")];
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .form(¶ms)
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#json)JSON

There is also a `json` method helper on the [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html) that works in
a similar fashion the

`form` method. It can take any value that can be
serialized into JSON.The feature `json` is required.

```
// This will POST a body of `{"lang":"rust","body":"json"}`
let mut map = HashMap::new();
map.insert("lang", "rust");
map.insert("body", "json");
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post")
    .json(&map)
    .send()
    .await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)Redirect Policies

By default, a `Client` will automatically handle HTTP redirects, having a
maximum redirect chain of 10 hops. To customize this behavior, a
[ redirect::Policy](https://docs.rs/redirect/index.html) can be used with a

`ClientBuilder`.[§](https://docs.rs#cookies)Cookies

The automatic storing and sending of session cookies can be enabled with
the [ cookie_store](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.cookie_store) method on

`ClientBuilder`.[§](https://docs.rs#proxies)Proxies

**NOTE**: System proxies are enabled by default.

System proxies look in environment variables to set HTTP or HTTPS proxies.

`HTTP_PROXY` or `http_proxy` provide HTTP proxies for HTTP connections while
`HTTPS_PROXY` or `https_proxy` provide HTTPS proxies for HTTPS connections.
`ALL_PROXY` or `all_proxy` provide proxies for both HTTP and HTTPS connections.
If both the all proxy and HTTP or HTTPS proxy variables are set the more specific
HTTP or HTTPS proxies take precedence.

These can be overwritten by adding a [ Proxy](https://docs.rs/struct.Proxy.html) to

`ClientBuilder`
i.e. `let proxy = reqwest::Proxy::http("https://secure.example")?;`
or disabled by calling `ClientBuilder::no_proxy()`.`socks` feature is required if you have configured socks proxy like this:

`export https_proxy=socks5://127.0.0.1:1086`[§](https://docs.rs#tls)TLS

A `Client` will use transport layer security (TLS) by default to connect to
HTTPS destinations.

- Additional server certificates can be configured on a `ClientBuilder`with the`Certificate`
- Client certificates can be added to a `ClientBuilder`with the`Identity`
- Various parts of TLS can also be configured or even disabled on the
`ClientBuilder`.

See more details in the [ tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm)WASM

The Client implementation automatically switches to the WASM one when the target_arch is wasm32,
the usage is basically the same as the async api. Some of the features are disabled in wasm
: [ tls](https://docs.rs/tls/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/cookie/index.html)

`cookie`[, as well as various](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)

`blocking``ClientBuilder` methods such as `timeout()` and `connector_layer()`.TLS and cookies are provided through the browser environment, so reqwest can issue TLS requests with cookies, but has limited configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

The following are a list of [Cargo features](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) that can be
enabled or disabled:

- **http2**- *(enabled by default)*: Enables HTTP/2 support.
- **default-tls**- *(enabled by default)*: Provides TLS support to connect over HTTPS.
- **rustls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`.
- **rustls-no-provider**: Enables TLS provided by- `rustls`without specifying a crypto provider.
- **native-tls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-vendored**: Enables the- `vendored`feature of- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-no-alpn**: Enables- `native-tls`without its- `alpn`feature.
- **native-tls-vendored-no-alpn**: Enables- `native-tls-vendored`without its- `alpn`feature.
- **blocking**: Provides the- [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)client API.
- **charset**- *(enabled by default)*: Improved support for decoding text.
- **cookies**: Provides cookie session support.
- **gzip**: Provides response body gzip decompression.
- **brotli**: Provides response body brotli decompression.
- **zstd**: Provides response body zstd decompression.
- **deflate**: Provides response body deflate decompression.
- **query**: Provides query parameter serialization.
- **form**: Provides form data serialization.
- **json**: Provides serialization and deserialization for JSON bodies.

- **socks**: Provides SOCKS5 proxy support.
- **hickory-dns**: Enables a hickory-dns async resolver instead of default threadpool using- `getaddrinfo`.
- **system-proxy**- *(enabled by default)*: Use Windows and macOS system proxy settings automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable Features

Some feature flags require additional opt-in by the application, by setting
a `reqwest_unstable` flag.

- **http3**- *(unstable)*: Enables support for sending HTTP/3 requests.

These features are unstable, and experimental. Details about them may be changed in patch releases.

You can pass such a flag to the compiler via `.cargo/config`, or
environment variables, such as:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg reqwest_unstable" cargo build`[§](https://docs.rs#sponsors)Sponsors

# uuid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/uuid/^1/

## Expand description

Generate and parse universally unique identifiers (UUIDs).

Here’s an example of a UUID:

`67e55044-10b1-426f-9247-bb680e5fe0c8`A UUID is a unique 128-bit value, stored as 16 octets, and regularly formatted as a hex string in five groups. UUIDs are used to assign unique identifiers to entities without requiring a central allocating authority.

They are particularly useful in distributed systems, though can be used in disparate areas, such as databases and network protocols. Typically a UUID is displayed in a readable string form as a sequence of hexadecimal digits, separated into groups by hyphens.

The uniqueness property is not strictly guaranteed, however for all practical purposes, it can be assumed that an unintentional collision would be extremely unlikely.

UUIDs have a number of standardized encodings that are specified in [RFC 9562](https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc9562.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add the following to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.uuid]
version = "1.23.4"
# Lets you generate random UUIDs
features = [
    "v4",
]
```
When you want a UUID, you can generate one:

```
use uuid::Uuid;
let id = Uuid::new_v4();
```
If you have a UUID value, you can use its string literal form inline:

```
use uuid::{uuid, Uuid};
const ID: Uuid = uuid!("67e55044-10b1-426f-9247-bb680e5fe0c8");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-different-uuid-versions)Working with different UUID versions

This library supports all standardized methods for generating UUIDs through individual Cargo features.

By default, this crate depends on nothing but the Rust standard library and can parse and format UUIDs, but cannot generate them. Depending on the kind of UUID you’d like to work with, there are Cargo features that enable generating them:

- `v1`- Version 1 UUIDs using a timestamp and monotonic counter.
- `v3`- Version 3 UUIDs based on the MD5 hash of some data.
- `v4`- Version 4 UUIDs with random data.
- `v5`- Version 5 UUIDs based on the SHA1 hash of some data.
- `v6`- Version 6 UUIDs using a timestamp and monotonic counter.
- `v7`- Version 7 UUIDs using a Unix timestamp.
- `v8`- Version 8 UUIDs using user-defined data.

This library also includes a [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) type that can be used to help construct UUIDs of any
version without any additional dependencies or features. It’s a lower-level API than

[that can be used when you need control over implicit requirements on things like a source of randomness.](https://docs.rs/struct.Uuid.html)

`Uuid`[§](https://docs.rs#which-uuid-version-should-i-use)Which UUID version should I use?

If you just want to generate unique identifiers then consider version 4 (`v4`) UUIDs. If you want
to use UUIDs as database keys or need to sort them then consider version 7 (`v7`) UUIDs.
Other versions should generally be avoided unless there’s an existing need for them.

Some UUID versions supersede others. Prefer version 6 over version 1 and version 5 over version 3.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-features)Other features

Other crate features can also be useful beyond the version support:

- `serde`- adds the ability to serialize and deserialize a UUID using- `serde`.
- `borsh`- adds the ability to serialize and deserialize a UUID using- `borsh`.
- `arbitrary`- adds an- `Arbitrary`trait implementation to- `Uuid`for fuzzing.
- `fast-rng`- uses a faster algorithm for generating random UUIDs when available. This feature requires more dependencies to compile, but is just as suitable for UUIDs as the default algorithm.
- `rng-rand`- forces- `rand`as the backend for randomness.
- `rng-getrandom`- forces- `getrandom`as the backend for randomness.
- `bytemuck`- adds a- `Pod`trait implementation to- `Uuid`for byte manipulation

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

Some features are unstable. They may be incomplete or depend on other unstable libraries. These include:

- `zerocopy`- adds support for zero-copy deserialization using the- `zerocopy`library.

Unstable features may break between minor releases.

To allow unstable features, you’ll need to enable the Cargo feature as
normal, but also pass an additional flag through your environment to opt-in
to unstable `uuid` features:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg uuid_unstable"`[§](https://docs.rs#building-for-other-targets)Building for other targets

[§](https://docs.rs#webassembly)WebAssembly

For WebAssembly, enable the `js` feature:

```
[dependencies.uuid]
version = "1.23.4"
features = [
    "v4",
    "v7",
    "js",
]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#embedded)Embedded

For embedded targets without the standard library, you’ll need to
disable default features when building `uuid`:

```
[dependencies.uuid]
version = "1.23.4"
default-features = false
```
Some additional features are supported in no-std environments:

- `v1`,- `v3`,- `v5`,- `v6`, and- `v8`.
- `serde`.

If you need to use `v4` or `v7` in a no-std environment, you’ll need to
produce random bytes yourself and then pass them to [ Builder::from_random_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.from_random_bytes)
without enabling the

`v4` or `v7` features.If you’re using `getrandom`, you can specify the `rng-getrandom` or `rng-rand`
features of `uuid` and configure `getrandom`’s provider per its docs. `uuid`
may upgrade its version of `getrandom` in minor releases.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Parse a UUID given in the simple format and print it as a URN:

```
let my_uuid = Uuid::parse_str("a1a2a3a4b1b2c1c2d1d2d3d4d5d6d7d8")?;
println!("{}", my_uuid.urn());
```
Generate a random UUID and print it out in hexadecimal form:

```
// Note that this requires the `v4` feature to be enabled.
let my_uuid = Uuid::new_v4();
println!("{}", my_uuid);
```

- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Strategies for combining delegate strategies into `std::Result`s.
- [sample](https://docs.rs/sample/index.html)
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of collections.
- [strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/index.html)
- Defines the core traits used by Proptest.
- [string](https://docs.rs/string/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating strings and byte strings from regular expressions.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_runner/index.html)- runner
- State and functions for running proptest tests.
- [tuple](https://docs.rs/tuple/index.html)
- Support for combining strategies into tuples.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert.html)- assert
- Similar to `assert!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Similar to `assert_eq!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Similar to `assert_ne!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assume.html)- assume
- Rejects the test input if assumptions are not met.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_compose.html)- compose
- Convenience to define functions which produce new strategies.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_oneof.html)- oneof
- Produce a strategy which picks one of the listed choices.
- [proptest](https://docs.rs/macro.proptest.html)
- Easily define `proptest`tests.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [property_](https://docs.rs/attr.property_test.html)- test - `attr-macro`
- The `property_test`procedural macro simplifies the creation of property-based tests using the`proptest`crate. This macro provides a more concise syntax for writing tests that automatically generate test cases based on properties.

# lash_provider_google::oauth - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lash-provider-google/0.1.0-alpha.82/lash_provider_google/oauth/index.html

## Expand description

Google OAuth authorize-URL / code-exchange / refresh-token flow.
Public so `lash-cli`’s setup UI can drive the interactive login.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [authorize_](https://docs.rs/fn.authorize_url.html)- url
- Build the Google OAuth authorization URL for manual code entry.
- [exchange_](https://docs.rs/fn.exchange_code.html)- code
- Exchange an authorization code (or a redirect URL containing
`code=...`) for tokens.
- [refresh_](https://docs.rs/fn.refresh_tokens.html)- tokens
- Refresh Google OAuth tokens.

# sim_kernel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

sim-kernel is the small protocol kernel of the SIM Rust runtime.

The kernel defines contracts; libraries supply behavior. This crate holds
the protocol and contract types – forms, values, stores, registry and
callable surfaces, the [ shape](https://docs.rs/shape/index.html) protocol, evaluation policy, and the ABI
transport – while concrete behavior (parsers, number domains, the standard
distribution, and server/agent/browse implementations) lives in separate
library crates loaded against these contracts. SIM is a Rust runtime, not a
Lisp runtime; Lisp is one codec surface among several.

The one deliberate exception is the pair of built-in *reference backends*:
[ list::VecList](https://docs.rs/list/struct.VecList.html) (a

[) and](https://docs.rs/list/trait.ListValue.html)

`list::ListValue`[(a](https://docs.rs/table/struct.AssocTable.html)

`table::AssocTable`[). These are the kernel’s bootstrap list and table implementations – minimal, correct, and self-annotated](https://docs.rs/table/trait.Table.html)

`table::Table``sim-non-citizen` –
so the runtime can stand up collections before any library loads. They are
reference implementations, not the only backends: alternatives load as libs
against the [/](https://docs.rs/list/trait.ListBackend.html)

`list::ListBackend`[contracts. (Future cleanup: move even these into a default-loaded distribution lib so the kernel ships pure contracts; tracked against the constellation reorg.)](https://docs.rs/table/trait.TableBackend.html)

`table::TableBackend`The kernel data flow is:

`tokens -> checked forms -> objects -> checked calls -> objects -> encoded forms`[§](https://docs.rs#module-map)Module map

Core forms and values: [ value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html),

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [callable](https://docs.rs/callable/index.html)
- The callable contract: objects that can be invoked with checked arguments.
- [capability](https://docs.rs/capability/index.html)
- Capability names and sets: the contract for gating privileged operations.
- [card](https://docs.rs/card/index.html)
- Card records: the contract for structured metadata about runtime subjects.
- [catalog](https://docs.rs/catalog/index.html)
- The registry catalog substrate: transactional, `Cx`-free table storage.
- [claim](https://docs.rs/claim/index.html)
- Claims: the contract for asserted facts about runtime subjects.
- [class](https://docs.rs/class/index.html)
- The class contract: callable factories with subclass relationships.
- [control](https://docs.rs/control/index.html)
- Control policy: the contract for delimited prompts, capture, and resume.
- [datum](https://docs.rs/datum/index.html)
- The `Datum`
- [datum_](https://docs.rs/datum_store/index.html)- store
- The `DatumStore`
- [effect](https://docs.rs/effect/index.html)
- The effect contract: capability-gated requests resolved by an implementation.
- [effect_](https://docs.rs/effect_ledger/index.html)- ledger
- The effect ledger: the contract for recording and replaying effects.
- [encode](https://docs.rs/encode/index.html)
- The encode contract: turning objects back into forms at a known position.
- [env](https://docs.rs/env/index.html)
- The evaluation environment: `Cx``Env`
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- The error and diagnostic contract for the kernel.
- [eval](https://docs.rs/eval/index.html)
- Evaluation policy and the macro-expander contract.
- [event](https://docs.rs/event/index.html)
- The event contract: timestamped records emitted during evaluation.
- [event_](https://docs.rs/event_ledger/index.html)- ledger
- The event ledger: the contract for accumulating ordered events by tick.
- [expr](https://docs.rs/expr/index.html)
- The `Expr`
- [fact_](https://docs.rs/fact_store/index.html)- store
- The `FactStore`
- [factory](https://docs.rs/factory/index.html)
- The factory contract: constructing runtime objects from data.
- [handle_](https://docs.rs/handle_store/index.html)- store
- The `HandleStore`
- [hint](https://docs.rs/hint/index.html)
- Open hint metadata for diagnostics, exports, and runtime operations.
- [id](https://docs.rs/id/index.html)
- Stable ids and the `Symbol`
- [library](https://docs.rs/library/index.html)
- The library and registry contracts: loading behavior against the kernel.
- [list](https://docs.rs/list/index.html)
- The list contract: the pluggable `ListValue`
- [native_](https://docs.rs/native_abi/index.html)- abi
- The native ABI: byte-frame and manifest transport types for dynamic libs.
- [number_](https://docs.rs/number_domain/index.html)- domain
- The number-domain contract: the pluggable numeric backend protocol.
- [object](https://docs.rs/object/index.html)
- The object contract: the runtime object surface and argument forms.
- [op](https://docs.rs/op/index.html)
- The operation contract: keyed, shape-checked calls dispatched on objects.
- [pratt](https://docs.rs/pratt/index.html)
- Pratt-parser contracts: operator tables for `shape`
- [rank](https://docs.rs/rank/index.html)
- Rank metadata: the contract for ordering and navigating ranked spaces.
- [realize](https://docs.rs/realize/index.html)
- The `realize`surface: the location-transparent distributed eval contract.
- [ref_id](https://docs.rs/ref_id/index.html)
- Reference identity: the `Ref`
- [ref_](https://docs.rs/ref_resolver/index.html)- resolver
- The `RefResolver`
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- The `Sequence`
- [shape](https://docs.rs/shape/index.html)
- The `Shape`
- [shape_](https://docs.rs/shape_report/index.html)- report
- Shape reports: the contract for diagnostics from `shape`
- [standard](https://docs.rs/standard/index.html)
- Standard-distribution metadata: the profile and organ claim vocabulary.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)
- The `Stream`

# sim_lib_music_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-music-core/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

Core music model layer for the SIM music constellation.

SIM is a Rust runtime with multiple codec surfaces; this crate supplies the concrete music domain that those surfaces operate on. It defines the music object model (notes, chords, melodies, scores), the descriptor metadata that describes music components and their ports and parameters, events and lanes, the piano roll and time grid, players and playables, performances and takes, the arranger, freeze surfaces, traces, the component registry, and the citizen integration that registers these types with the runtime.

# sim_lib_pitch_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-core/^0.1.0-rc.1/

## Expand description

Core pitch theory primitives for the SIM music libraries.

This crate defines the foundational pitch types shared across the `sim-lib-pitch-*`
constellation: the mod-12 [ PitchClass](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchClass.html), the octave-aware

[, the letter-plus-accidental](https://docs.rs/struct.Pitch.html)

`Pitch`[, and the](https://docs.rs/struct.SpelledPitch.html)

`SpelledPitch`[measured in semitones. Higher-level crates (sets, scales, chords, namers) build on these primitives rather than redefining their own pitch representations.](https://docs.rs/struct.Interval.html)

`Interval`Pitch classes use the twelve-tone equal-tempered convention where `C = 0` and
values increase by semitone up to `B = 11`. Octave-aware pitches use the MIDI
convention in which middle C (`C4`) is MIDI note 60.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Interval](https://docs.rs/struct.Interval.html)
- A pitch interval measured in semitones.
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.Pitch.html)
- An octave-aware pitch: a `PitchClass`
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchClass.html)- Class
- A mod-12 pitch class, where `C = 0`and values increase by semitone to`B = 11`.
- [Spelled](https://docs.rs/struct.SpelledPitch.html)- Pitch
- A spelled pitch: a diatonic `Letter`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Letter](https://docs.rs/enum.Letter.html)
- A diatonic letter name, independent of accidental.
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/enum.PitchError.html)- Error
- Error returned when a pitch, pitch class, or interval cannot be constructed or parsed.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_interval.html)- interval
- Parses one of the recognized interval tokens (`"P5"`,`"m3"`,`"M7"`,`"TT"`) into an`Interval`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_pitch.html)- pitch
- Parses a pitch spelling such as `"C4"`,`"Eb5"`, or`"Cs4"`into a`Pitch`
